sample_unit: participants (10 ophthalmologists, 10 residents, 10 senior medical students), each completing 30 cases

links.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of clinicians with vs without LLM collaboration compared with LLM-only accuracy
links.effect: Accuracy rose from 0.45 to 0.60 with HAC (P<0.001); 20% of participants declined; HAC mean stayed below LLM-only accuracy (0.70).
links.quote: HAC significantly improved mean accuracy compared to the human-only condition (from 0.45 to 0.60, P < 0.001), although 20% of participants showed a decline in performance and the mean remained below the LLM-only accuracy (0.70).

links.outcome: Whether users accepted incorrect LLM insights in failed human-AI collaboration
links.effect: 58.6% of failed HAC involved the LLM presenting incorrect insight and the human accepting it; 92.6% of successes involved correct insight accepted.
links.quote: In successful HAC, 92.6% followed the pattern LLM presents correct insight/human accepts, while 58.6% of failures involved LLM presents incorrect insight/human accepts.

unlisted_practices: Targeting human-LLM collaboration to tasks where baseline human accuracy is adequate, based on task difficulty

screen.reason: The study empirically tests human-AI collaboration (clinician review/interaction with Claude-3.5-Sonnet) versus human-alone in an experimental vignette study of 30 challenging clinical cases.
